grammar.title: Frase
grammar.rule: Paulo pegou o caderno. Ana e Bia colocaram o mapa na mesa. Ontem preparamos o plano.
grammar.note_en:
This chapter introduces the completed past for regular -ar verbs. Portuguese often calls this the pretérito perfeito. Here it presents an action as a completed event rather than something currently in progress. Paulo pegou o caderno means “Paulo took the notebook”; colocou o caderno na mesa means “he put the notebook on the table.” Both actions are completed; Agora está procurando a página cinco means “Now he is looking for page five.” The new ending helps reconstruct movements instead of merely adding a time label to an unchanged present verb.

For the forms actually encountered here, use the regular endings -ei for eu, -ou for a singular name or você, -amos for nós, and -aram for a plural subject, making the spelling adjustments described below. Peguei means “I took”; pegou, “he/she/you took.” Guardei means “I kept/stored”; guardou, “he/she/you kept/stored.” Visitei o Café da Ponte means “I visited the Café da Ponte”; Paulo visitou o segundo café means “Paulo visited the second café.” Colocaram o mapa na mesa means “They put the map on the table.” Each production item uses an actual cell read before that section’s practice; a class pattern does not license an unseen answer by itself.

Before -ei, spelling changes preserve pronunciation in three encountered verbs: pegar gives peguei (“I took”), keeping the hard g sound; colocar gives coloquei (“I placed”), keeping the k sound; pagar likewise gives paguei (“I paid”), keeping hard g. The usual written stem cannot simply remain unchanged before e. The story contrasts Paguei uma conta ontem (“I paid a bill yesterday”) with A cliente pagou a conta (“The customer paid the bill”). The extra letter is a spelling requirement, not a different tense. This chapter teaches only the forms read here, not an unrestricted spelling paradigm for every similar verb. Fechei means “I closed”; fechou, “he/she/you closed”; fechei o caderno means “I closed the notebook.” The already known fechado describes the closed state; the new verb names the action producing that state.

The -amos form can be identical to the earlier present form in Brazilian Portuguese. Ontem preparamos o plano no papel means “Yesterday we prepared the plan on paper.” Its completed-past reading comes from the whole account of finished planning, not from a special printed accent. The same familiar preparamos can mean “we prepare” in a present account. Do not manufacture an accent to distinguish them. The story also uses Ana e Bia prepararam (“Ana and Bia prepared”) and limparam (“they cleaned”) for completed plural actions. The final vowel and ending do not change with a feminine subject.

Completed past is not restricted to yesterday. Hoje de manhã, Ana e Bia limparam o chão means “This morning Ana and Bia cleaned the floor”; o vizinho consertou o buraco do telhado means “the neighbor repaired the hole in the roof.” Those Saturday tasks are finished before the notebook search, even though the same day continues. Compare Rosa está servindo uma cliente (“Rosa is serving a customer”): service is currently in progress. Amanhã is not needed for every future statement, and ontem does not itself create a past tense. Use the tense and the situation together.

This target is deliberately restricted to -ar verbs. Perder means “to lose,” and esquecer “to forget”; their -er completed-past forms are not taught here. The chapter instead uses known modal or present frames: Não quero perder o recibo means “I do not want to lose the receipt”; Não quero esquecer os nomes dos cafés means “I do not want to forget the cafés’ names”; Paulo esquece os nomes means “Paulo forgets the names.” Lembrar means “to remember”; Não lembro meu caminho de ontem means “I do not remember my route yesterday.” These examples take a direct noun object. No reflexive pronoun, complement with que, irregular past, or new recipient construction is introduced.

The documents do different jobs. Conta means “bill”: it states what is to be paid. Recibo means “receipt”: it records the payment afterward. Guardar o recibo means “to keep the receipt safe”; perder o recibo, “to lose the receipt.” A receipt can cue Paulo’s remembered visit, but its hour is the café/payment hour, not proof of when a page left a notebook. The chapter checks the day as well as the name. The printed five is a fictional amount without a new currency-unit word; no real-world price or opening-hour claim is made.

Uma semana means “one week.” The delivered two-row calendar groups seven days in each week. Its numbers are fictional calendar dates, unlike the earlier reference’s positions within a week. Here today is Saturday13, yesterday is Friday12, and Saturday6 belongs to the previous week. Semana passada means “last week”; sábado passado means “last Saturday.” Passada agrees with feminine semana and passado with masculine sábado. A day can be in the past without being in the previous week: yesterday Friday12 and today Saturday13 share a week. That distinction rejects the wrong receipt rather than merely demonstrating a word list.

Novamente means “again.” Paulo opens the notebook after closing it, and Ana reads the receipt a second time. The word points to a repeated action, not a change of tense or an instruction to repeat every sentence. The whole notebook is now present; only page five is missing. The visit and return on Friday are reconstructed with regular -ar forms, while the page’s mover, location and authorship remain unknown. The second café and its hours are fictional story evidence, not real travel or business advice.
